fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Ravid. What I value most about that study is honestly not the final model. It's the process we forced ourselves to go through to get there.

When we started, the narrative in the field was that transformers had "won" vision, and the implicit explanation was that attention is somehow fundamentally better than convolution. But if you looked at how a Swin Transformer was actually trained versus how a ResNet-50 had been trained in 2015, almost everything was different. The optimizer, the data augmentation, the regularization, the schedule, the stage ratios, the stem, the normalization layers, the activation functions. People were comparing a modern recipe to a decade-old baseline and attributing the whole gap to the architecture.

So the thing I'm proudest of is that we refused to make one big jump. We took a standard ResNet and changed exactly one thing at a time, in a fixed order, and measured each step. Just updating the training recipe, with no architectural change at all, took ResNet-50 from roughly 76 percent to around 78 percent on ImageNet. That alone told you a large part of the story. Then each design decision, like going to depthwise convolutions, inverting the bottleneck, enlarging the kernel to seven by seven, swapping BatchNorm for LayerNorm, swapping ReLU for GELU, and using fewer of them, contributed its own small, quantifiable piece.

What that gives you is a roadmap rather than a result. Anyone can read the paper and see which choices mattered, which barely mattered, and which were just borrowed from transformers because they happened to be there. Several of those ideas were not new at all. Depthwise convolutions, inverted bottlenecks, large kernels, these had all appeared before, often in the mobile network literature. The contribution was putting them together under a controlled comparison and showing that a pure ConvNet, with no attention at all, could match or beat Swin at the same compute, on classification, detection, and segmentation, and scale just as well.

The broader lesson I keep coming back to is about how we do science in this field. Architectural comparisons are only meaningful when the rest of the system is held fixed, and most of our "which architecture is better" debates are really confounded by training recipes. I also think it was healthy for the community to see that the inductive biases of convolution, like translation equivariance and locality, were not a liability. They're still a very good prior, and the simplicity of the resulting model, which is just a stack of standard blocks with no relative position biases or shifted windows, made it easy for people to adopt and build on.

So if I had to summarize it in one line, the result I value is not "ConvNets are back." It's that we showed how to ask the question properly.

r001.rationale: The response says the study’s value was correcting the belief that attention alone explained the performance gap and showing that comparisons were confounded by training recipes. It presents the component measurements as supporting that broader change in understanding.

r002.rationale: The response calls locality a useful inductive bias, but does not say it gives ConvNets an advantage when processing high-resolution images.

opus-5.5.text:
I think what I value most is the methodology itself: the roadmap we followed. When vision transformers came out, and especially when Swin Transformer started beating ConvNets on detection and segmentation, the prevailing story was that attention was the key and convolution had hit its limit. But when you compared a ViT or Swin to a ResNet, you weren't comparing just two architectures. You were comparing two whole packages. The transformer side had a new training recipe with AdamW, much longer training, and heavy augmentation like Mixup, CutMix and RandAugment. It also had different macro design choices and different normalization and activation functions. So many things changed at once that you couldn't really tell where the gains came from.

What we did was start from a standard ResNet-50 and modernize it one step at a time, measuring the effect of each change. First we just updated the training recipe, and that alone gave a surprisingly large boost. Then we changed the stage compute ratio and used a patchify stem. We added depthwise convolutions, an inverted bottleneck, and larger kernels like 7×7. Then came the micro details: GELU instead of ReLU, fewer activations and normalization layers, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm, and separate downsampling layers. None of these ideas were individually new. But taken together, a pure ConvNet ended up matching or exceeding Swin with essentially no attention.

So the part I value most isn't really the final model. It's the lesson that a lot of what we credited to the transformer was actually coming from the training procedure and design details, not from self-attention itself. For me that was a reminder to be careful about the narratives the field tells itself. When a new architecture wins, it's worth asking which ingredient is actually responsible. Often the answer is more mundane and more interesting than you expect.

I also like that the result is simple. ConvNeXt has no fancy new modules. It's a clean ConvNet that people can understand, reproduce and build on. I think that clarity is a big part of why it was useful to people.

r001.rationale: The response frames the study’s main value as revising the belief that self-attention drove the gains, crediting training and design choices instead. It mentions measuring individual changes, but presents the broader shift in understanding as the key lesson.

fable-5.text:
Thanks for having me, Ravid. I think what I value most about that work is actually not the model itself, but what the process taught us about how we attribute progress in the field.

When vision transformers came out, the narrative very quickly became that attention was the key ingredient, that ConvNets were fundamentally limited and this new architecture class had simply surpassed them. What we did in the ConvNeXt study was essentially a controlled experiment: we took a standard ResNet and, step by step, modernized it — the training recipe, the stage compute ratios, the larger kernel sizes, the activation functions, the normalization layers, moving to fewer activations and norms the way transformers do. And at each step we measured exactly how much each change contributed.

What we found was that most of the gap between ConvNets and vision transformers came from these design and training details, not from attention per se. A pure ConvNet, carefully modernized, could match or exceed Swin Transformers across classification, detection, and segmentation.

To me, the lasting value is twofold. First, it's a reminder that we often conflate the contribution of an architecture with the contribution of everything around it — the recipe, the augmentations, the optimization. If you don't do the careful ablation, you end up drawing the wrong scientific conclusions. And second, I hope it showed that simplicity still has a place. ConvNeXt is deliberately simple — no novel modules, no attention, just standard components arranged carefully. The fact that something that simple remains competitive tells you a lot about where the real progress in the field actually comes from.

opus-5.text:
What I value most isn't really the final model — it's the discipline of the process. When ConvNeXt came out, the prevailing story was that self-attention was the reason vision transformers were winning. But when you actually looked at what had changed between a ResNet from 2015 and a Swin Transformer from 2021, it wasn't just attention. The training recipe was completely different — AdamW instead of SGD, 300 epochs instead of 90, RandAugment, Mixup, stochastic depth, label smoothing. The macro design was different. The normalization and activation choices were different. All of that was bundled together and credited to one component.

So we tried to take the bundle apart and move one piece at a time, keeping everything else fixed, and reporting the number after each step. That's not glamorous work. There's no new module in the paper that you can name. But I think the most useful thing we did was show how much of the perceived gap was attribution error, and that a pure convolutional network, modernized carefully, lands in the same place.

The lesson I carry from it is that in our field we're often comparing systems, not ideas, and then telling ourselves stories about the ideas. Whenever someone says a new architectural primitive gave them two points, my first question now is: what else changed? Usually quite a lot.

sonnet-5.5.text:
What I value most is that it showed how much of the "transformers versus ConvNets" story was really about details nobody had isolated. When vision transformers took off, the common explanation was that attention is fundamentally better than convolution. But a lot of things changed at once: the architecture, the training recipe, the data augmentation, the optimizer, the macro design of the network. It was hard to say which of those actually mattered.

So we did something fairly simple. We started with a standard ResNet and moved it toward a transformer-style design one step at a time, changing one thing and measuring the effect. We updated the training recipe, adjusted the stage ratios and the patchify stem, used depthwise convolution, an inverted bottleneck, larger kernels, and swapped BatchNorm for LayerNorm and ReLU for GELU. At the end, a pure ConvNet matched or beat the vision transformers of that time, and it was still just a convolutional network.

I'm proud of that kind of careful, controlled comparison. It isn't a flashy new idea. It tells you which pieces matter and which are just folklore. I think the field needs more of that, especially when everyone is excited about a new direction and tempted to credit the headline component, like attention, when a good part of the gain comes from the surrounding design and training choices.

It also changed how I think about research. A lot of progress comes from understanding and cleaning up what we already have, not only from inventing something new. If the conclusion is that the differences are smaller than people thought, that's still a useful result, because it points you toward the factors that really drive performance.

haiku-5.5.text:
What I value most is being forced to ask an unglamorous question: when one model beats another, is it really the architecture? We kept finding that much of what people credited to attention or the transformer block was coming from everything around it, like the training recipe, the augmentation, the optimizer settings, and how the network was scaled. When we changed one thing at a time and gradually modernized a plain convolutional network, the gap largely closed, and several design choices borrowed from transformers turned out to be useful on their own.

I like that kind of accounting because it doesn't crown a winner. It tells you which ingredients matter. It also gave me more respect for the simple baseline. A convolutional network comes with strong assumptions built in, like locality and translation equivariance. Those aren't limitations to apologize for. They're useful priors, and you can keep them while still getting the benefits people associated with newer designs.

There's a practical payoff too. When the comparison is clean, people can build on the result instead of arguing about whose tricks are better. That's the part I find most satisfying.
